`const name = user.name` writes `name` twice. `const { name } = user` writes it once, and the next property you need goes into the same statement.

This is `prefer-destructuring` with types. `const [first] = items` only works if `items` can be iterated, so `items[0]` is reported only when the type of `items` is iterable or `any`. A declaration with a type annotation is left alone by default.

With `bunfig.toml`, turning this rule on runs it in TypeScript files and `prefer-destructuring` in JavaScript files, so nothing is reported twice. With an ESLint config, turn the other rule off when you use this one.

A property is only reported if the variable has the same name. An element is only reported if the index is a literal whole number, such as `items[0]`.

`--fix` rewrites `const name = user.name`. Elements and plain assignments are reported but not fixed.

{/* Generated by src/codegen/lint-rule-docs.ts. Do not edit this section. */}

## Configure

Off by default. This rule needs types, so turning it on makes `bun lint` type check your code first.

```toml bunfig.toml
[lint.rules]
"@typescript-eslint/prefer-destructuring" = "error" # or "warn"
```

Every option, set to its default. The ones that are commented out are unset by default.

```toml bunfig.toml
[lint.rules]
"@typescript-eslint/prefer-destructuring" = [
  "error",
  {
    AssignmentExpression = { array = true, object = true },
    VariableDeclarator = { array = true, object = true },
    # object = true,
    # array = true,
  },
  {
    enforceForRenamedProperties = false,
    enforceForDeclarationWithTypeAnnotation = false,
  },
]
```

{/* End of the generated section. */}

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad {"count": 3} */}
```ts
declare const user: { name: string; email: string };
declare const items: string[];
let email: string;

const name = user.name;
const first = items[0];
email = user.email;
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```ts
declare const user: { name: string; email: string };
declare const items: string[];
declare const scores: { 0: number; 1: number };
let email: string;

const { name } = user;
const [first] = items;
({ email } = user);

const best = scores[0]; // not iterable
const label: string = user.name; // has a type annotation
```

## Options

The rule takes two objects. The first says what to check, and the second has the two `enforceFor` options.

```toml bunfig.toml
[lint.rules]
"@typescript-eslint/prefer-destructuring" = [
  "error",
  { object = true, array = false },
  { enforceForRenamedProperties = true },
]
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `object` | `true` | Report properties: `const name = user.name`. |
| `array` | `true` | Report elements: `const first = items[0]`. |
| `enforceForRenamedProperties` | `false` | Also report a property that goes into a variable with another name, a computed key, and a number key of an object that isn't iterable. |
| `enforceForDeclarationWithTypeAnnotation` | `false` | Also report declarations that have a type annotation. They aren't fixed. |

If you pass the first object, a key you leave out is `false`. With `{ object: true }`, elements aren't reported:

{/* good {"options": [{"object": true}]} */}
```ts
declare const items: string[];

const first = items[0];
```

With `enforceForRenamedProperties`, both of these are reported:

{/* bad {"options": [{"object": true}, {"enforceForRenamedProperties": true}], "count": 2} */}
```ts
declare const user: { name: string };
declare const scores: { 0: number; 1: number };

const label = user.name;
const best = scores[0];
```

With `enforceForDeclarationWithTypeAnnotation`, this is reported too:

{/* bad {"options": [{"object": true}, {"enforceForDeclarationWithTypeAnnotation": true}]} */}
```ts
declare const user: { name: string };

const name: string = user.name;
```

To treat declarations and assignments differently, give the first object the keys `VariableDeclarator` and `AssignmentExpression`, each with its own `object` and `array`. With both off for `AssignmentExpression`, this isn't reported:

{/* good {"options": [{"VariableDeclarator": {"object": true, "array": true}, "AssignmentExpression": {"object": false, "array": false}}]} */}
```ts
declare const user: { email: string };
let email: string;

email = user.email;
```
